passage_text: Researchers at the University of Health Sciences investigated the effect of a new antihypertensive medication on systolic blood pressure. Forty-eight adults aged 45-65 with mild hypertension were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a placebo control, a low-dose group (25 mg), a medium-dose group (50 mg), and a high-dose group (75 mg). Baseline systolic blood pressure was measured for all participants. Over a four-week period, participants took their assigned medication daily. After the intervention, systolic blood pressure was measured again. The results are summarized in Table 1. The data show a dose-dependent decrease in systolic blood pressure, with the high-dose group experiencing the greatest reduction. No serious adverse events were reported. These findings suggest that the medication may be effective in lowering blood pressure in a dose-responsive manner, but further studies are needed to assess long-term safety and efficacy. The study employed a double-blind, randomized controlled design to minimize bias. Blood pressure readings were taken using calibrated sphygmomanometers at baseline and at the end of the study. Statistical analysis revealed that the high-dose group had a mean reduction of 22 mmHg (p<0.01 versus placebo, whose own reduction was 2 mmHg). The low- and medium-dose groups showed reductions of 8 mmHg and 16 mmHg, respectively, both statistically significant (p<0.05). No participants reported dizziness or headache, suggesting a favorable tolerability profile.
table_data:
Group | Baseline BP (mmHg) | 4-week BP (mmHg) | Change (mmHg)
Control | 140 | 138 | -2
Low Dose | 140 | 132 | -8
Medium Dose | 140 | 124 | -16
High Dose | 140 | 118 | -22
stem: Which group experienced the greatest reduction in systolic blood pressure?
explanation: The high-dose group showed a 22 mmHg reduction, the largest among all groups.
trap: Some may incorrectly assume the low-dose group had the greatest reduction because it is the first non-placebo group listed.

stem: Which experimental design best controls for placebo effect in this study?
explanation: A randomized double-blind design ensures neither participants nor investigators know group assignments, reducing placebo bias.
trap: A crossover design may also reduce placebo effects but was not used in this study.

stem: What is the percent reduction in systolic blood pressure for the Medium Dose group?
trap: Dividing the 16 mmHg drop by the follow-up value (124 mmHg) gives 12.9% instead of dividing by the starting value of 140 mmHg.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a valid conclusion from the data?

options.A: High dose reduces blood pressure significantly
options.B: Medium dose lowers blood pressure more than low dose
options.D: High dose is better than low dose

explanation: The low-dose group had an 8 mmHg reduction (vs 2 mmHg in control), so 'low dose has no effect' is not valid. A, B and D are supported by the table (22 and 16 mmHg vs 8 mmHg).
trap: The wording 'no effect' can mislead readers into thinking the low dose is ineffective.

stem: By how many mmHg did the High Dose group’s SBP reduction exceed the Control group’s reduction?
explanation: Correct: A) High dose changed by -22 and control by -2, so the excess reduction is 22 - 2 = 20 mmHg. Why the others are wrong: B) 22 mmHg is the raw high-dose change and ignores the control change. C) 24 mmHg adds the control change instead of subtracting it. D) 14 mmHg is 22 - 8, the difference from the low dose rather than from control.
trap: Reporting the raw 22 mmHg drop as the effect without subtracting the 2 mmHg fall seen in the control group.
